verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 131 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush prints it as 131). NOT 2.127: our id and label are off by four.
attribution_note: Valmiki to Ram, closing his list of the hearts Ram should live in, when Ram asks him where to stay in the forest.
translation_note: Accurate. 'sahaj sanehu' is natural, unforced affection rather than a decision to love; 'nij gehu' is your own house, the private home rather than one of many lodgings.
context: Ram, entering the forest, asks Valmiki where he should make his dwelling. Valmiki answers with a long list of the kinds of hearts Ram lives in (those whose ears are oceans for his story, whose eyes are thirsty for him, and so on). This doha is the last item in that list; right after it Tulsidas says the sage showed Ram these 'houses' and Ram was pleased, then Valmiki names Chitrakoot as the physical place to stay.

key_terms.sense: one who never wants anything at all (from you)
natural, unforced affection, love with no reason behind it
your very own house, your private home

core_teaching: The heart that loves without asking for anything back is where the divine is most at home. Wanting nothing is what makes the love 'one's own house' rather than a guest room.

commentaries.gist: Reads the love as like a parent's for an infant: it expects nothing and is happy in the child's happiness. A servant, friend or spouse loves with some expectation; only this kind is fully free of wanting.

commentaries.who: Earlier mahatmas, as reported in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Some read 'nij gehu' as Ram's private inner chamber and so take the doha as describing the sweetest, most intimate devotion (madhurya bhava).

commentaries.who: Sudarshan Singh, in Manas Piyush (on 'nij gehu')
commentaries.gist: Taking the speaker Valmiki as a father figure, 'your own house' means a paternal home: Ram need ask no one's leave to live there, and if it is not fit, making it fit is his own job.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to describe love that is not a transaction: being with someone or something for its own sake, not for what it gives. It also works as a quiet check on prayer that is mostly a list of requests.
misreadings: Not a rule that you must never ask God or anyone for help: it describes the highest kind of love, not a ban on need.
Not a statement that people who want things are unloved.
cautions: Devotional address to Ram; a secular reader may need it framed as 'love with no agenda'.
speaks_to: wanting a relationship that isn't transactional
someone tired of prayer that feels like bargaining
not_for: someone in acute need who may hear it as 'don't ask for help'
a person being exploited by someone who demands selfless love

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 150, chaupais 3-4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush prints the four lines as 150.5-8). NOT 2.146, and our text covers two chaupais, not one.
attribution_note: Sumantra to Dasharath, after returning without Ram.
translation_note: Faithful. 'Gosain' is a respectful address ('my lord'), not 'you who care for everyone'; that phrase translates 'sakal hitkari', which follows. Fine as is.
context: Sumantra comes back from leaving Ram, Lakshman and Sita at the Ganga. The king keeps asking for his son's message and begs him to bring them back into sight. Sumantra steadies himself and first reminds the king that he is learned, brave and steady, then offers this teaching. Immediately after, he relays Ram's messages; the king cannot bear it and dies a few dohas later.

key_terms.sense: under the sway of time and karma
unstoppably, the way night and day come
dull, unthinking (the opposite of the dhira)

core_teaching: Pleasure and pain, gain and loss, union and separation arrive by time and karma as surely as day follows night. The steady person holds both alike and uses discernment to hold on to courage.

commentaries.gist: Day following night cannot be held back by anyone; in the same way what time and karma bring must be lived through. Loss now may be followed by gain later.
The line about fools rejoicing and wailing is true in general but not of grief for Sita and Ram. Dasharath is no fool; Sumantra speaks because he fears the king will die of this love.
Grief destroys discernment and steadiness, so let it go; reflect with the understanding gained from guru and scripture and steadiness will follow.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to name the rhythm of life: good and bad turns come in cycles, and composure means not being thrown entirely by either. Discernment is the tool, not suppression.
misreadings: Not a claim that grief is foolish: the commentators say this very grief for Ram is not folly.
Not fatalism that excuses inaction; it addresses what has already happened.
cautions: Spoken to a man who dies of grief soon after: the advice did not save him. Using it on Day 1 of grief risks sounding like 'be stoic'.
'Fools rejoice and wail' can sting someone who is crying.
speaks_to: riding out a run of bad news
perspective after a setback at work or in money
someone who tends to swing high and low with events
not_for: fresh bereavement
someone who needs permission to cry rather than counsel to be steady
research_note: Our 'line' paraphrase is fine. Our_note's point that the king cannot take it in is supported by the narrative and by Pt. Ramkumar's note.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 165, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 165.5-6). NOT 2.159: our id and label are off by six.
attribution_note: Kausalya to Bharat, with him on her lap.
translation_note: Close. 'bali' is a mother's endearment ('may I be sacrificed for you'), not 'bless you', but the sense of tenderness is right. 'ghalani' is self-reproach.
context: Bharat has come home, learned what his mother did, and gone to Kausalya calling himself a stain on the family. She takes him on her lap, wipes his tears and says this. In the next lines she tells him not to blame anyone, including Kaikeyi, and puts the blame on her own fate instead.

key_terms.sense: calf, child; a mother's pet name
a bad time, an evil hour
the course of time and karma that cannot be altered

core_teaching: In a terrible time, hold on and let go of self-blame: what time and karma bring cannot be undone. The comfort comes from the one most wronged.

commentaries.gist: Bharat has been calling himself cursed and is still weeping; these are signs of losing composure, so she asks for steadiness even now, after a king's death and the exile.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji and Ramayan Prakash, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'See the bad time' means troubles come to everyone and also pass; in an evil hour grief is the only harvest, so set it down.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: She answers Bharat's two complaints in order: don't reproach yourself, and don't blame Kaikeyi either; then she takes the fault onto her own fate.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for someone crushed by guilt over harm others caused: the one who lost most refuses to blame them. It models comfort that removes shame without arguing.
misreadings: Not a denial that real wrongs happened; Kausalya names the loss as loss.
Not a reason to dodge one's own real responsibility (our misuse note is right).
cautions: Mentions a death in the family. The 'karma cannot be altered' framing can feel fatalistic to a newly bereaved reader.
speaks_to: guilt over a family member's wrongdoing
being forgiven by the person you expected to blame you
not_for: someone who actually caused harm and needs to own it
a reader who hears karma as blame for their loss

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 171, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 171.7-8). NOT 2.165.
attribution_note: Narration about Vasishtha. The speaker field 'Narrator' is right; listener blank is fine.
translation_note: Accurate. 'pulakeu' is horripilation (hair standing on end), which our 'trembled' softens; consider 'his body thrilled'.
context: After Dasharath's funeral rites, Vasishtha gathers the court and Bharat. Before advising Bharat to rule, he speaks of Ram's goodness and of Lakshman's and Sita's love, and is overcome. The next doha has him say, still weeping, that what is destined is powerful.

key_terms.sense: Ram's virtues, gentle conduct and nature
the sage, a man of knowledge

core_teaching: Even the wisest teacher is overwhelmed by grief and love; wisdom does not remove feeling. The Manas presents this as the greatness of love for Sita and Ram.

commentaries.who: Ramayan Prakash and Panjabi ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram's 'virtue, gentleness and nature' means how he obeyed his father gladly and said nothing harsh to Kaikeyi even after her cruel words.
A jnani should be beyond grief and attachment, yet the author of the Yoga Vasishtha sinks in both. This shows how strong the love for Ram, Sita and Lakshman is.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that composure and tears can coexist: the person who has to hold everyone together is allowed to grieve too.
misreadings: Not a sign that wisdom failed: the commentators read it as love's power, not weakness.
cautions: Set right after a funeral; gentle but it is grief context.
speaks_to: leaders or elders who feel they must not cry
grieving a person while having to manage others' grief
not_for: someone looking for practical steps

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 171 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 171). NOT 2.165.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Bharat.
translation_note: Accurate. 'bilakhi' is read two ways by commentators (see below); 'himself in tears' is the common reading. 'bidhi' is Providence or the Creator.
context: Vasishtha has just broken down while praising Ram, Lakshman and Sita. Now he speaks to Bharat: destiny is strong, and the six pairs of outcomes lie with Providence. The next line draws the conclusion: so whom should we blame, and at whom be angry in vain? He then urges Bharat to carry out his father's wish and rule.

key_terms.sense: what is bound to happen is powerful
in distress (or, per one reading, after careful consideration)

key_terms.term: हानि लाभु जीवनु मरनु जसु अपजसु
key_terms.sense: loss and gain, life and death, fame and infamy

core_teaching: Outcomes like loss, death and disgrace are not finally in our control. The point, made explicit in the next line, is that there is no one to blame and no use in anger.

commentaries.gist: 'Bilakhi' can mean sadly, since even the guru could not prevent this, or 'having considered closely', pre-empting Bharat's question why the guru let it happen.
Prefers 'grieving': even Vasishtha, son of the Creator, could not hold this back, and he speaks in sorrow. The other reading is strained.
Each of the six pairs plays out in this very story: Ayodhya's loss and the forest-dwellers' gain, Ravana's death, Bharat's fame and Kaikeyi's infamy.

commentaries.who: Nange Paramhans ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The real targets are three: the exile (loss), the king's death and Kaikeyi's disgrace. The opposites are named because these words come as pairs.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to release someone from blaming themselves or others for what was beyond anyone's control, so that grief does not turn into anger or guilt.
misreadings: Not an excuse for inaction or for not taking responsibility (our misuse note is apt).
Not a claim that nothing we do matters.
cautions: Names death directly. 'It was destined' can feel dismissive to a fresh mourner unless framed as freeing them from blame.
speaks_to: blaming yourself for an outcome you couldn't control
anger looking for a target after a loss
not_for: someone who is avoiding responsibility for a real choice
acute fresh grief where 'destiny' sounds cold

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 177, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 177.5-6). NOT 2.170 and NOT chaupai 7: both numbers in our id are wrong.
attribution_note: Bharat to the assembly. He is answering Vasishtha's counsel, which Kausalya and the ministers have backed; 'Vasishtha and Kausalya' is acceptable, though the 'you' here is mainly the guru and the elders together.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Vasishtha, the ministers and Kausalya have all urged Bharat to take the throne as his father wished. Bharat grants that their advice is simple and good for him, but says his heart is not satisfied. He then asks pardon for answering back, says suffering people's words should not be weighed, and argues that his only good is serving Ram; without Ram the kingdom is a heap of grief.

key_terms.sense: following which would do me good

core_teaching: Bharat admits that sound advice and inner peace can come apart: he understands the counsel but cannot be at peace with it, and says so openly and respectfully.

commentaries.gist: Glosses 'acharat' as 'by following it'. In the next line Bharat asks them to give him advice fit for him ('anuharat'), and asks pardon, since good people don't count a sufferer's words against him.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (meaning of the doha that follows)
commentaries.gist: Bharat then asks whether they think a kingdom is his good or their own convenience: his good lies only in serving Ram, which his mother's crookedness took away.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for the gap between knowing and feeling: you can agree with good advice and still not be at peace, and saying so honestly is better than pretending.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of elders' advice: Bharat praises it before declining it.
speaks_to: advice you agree with but can't make yourself follow
decisions where duty and heart pull apart
not_for: someone looking for permission to ignore all advice
research_note: Commentary on this specific line in Manas Piyush is thin (mostly the meaning). The second 'commentary' item is the Manas Piyush gloss of the following doha, which completes Bharat's argument.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 183, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 183.3-4). NOT 2.176.
attribution_note: Bharat to the assembly (and to himself).
translation_note: Accurate. 'anabhal' is bad, ill-doing; 'upadhi' is calamity, trouble.
context: Bharat has resolved to go to Ram. Just before, he says he can see no other remedy and will set out at dawn. Here he admits that the calamity happened because of him, yet trusts that Ram, seeing him come for refuge, will forgive. Next he describes Ram's gentle nature (he never harmed even an enemy) and asks the assembly for its blessing.
core_teaching: Admitting fault and trusting forgiveness are not opposites: coming face to face, for refuge, is what opens the way to being forgiven.

commentaries.gist: Ram has always been kind; going to him for refuge will bring 'special' kindness, which the commentator identifies with Ram later giving Bharat his sandals.
Compares other Manas lines where taking refuge saves even great sinners, and where a tiger is said not to eat one who faces it as a supplicant.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for going to someone you've hurt (or believe you've hurt), owning your part without excuses, and trusting their goodness rather than rehearsing defences.
misreadings: Not a claim that Bharat was actually guilty: the tradition treats his self-accusation as humility (our note is right).
Not a guarantee that every wronged person will forgive.
cautions: Someone with harsh, unfounded self-blame may take 'I am guilty' as confirmation.
speaks_to: guilt that keeps you from approaching someone
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship who is told to keep going back

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 192, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 192.7-8). NOT 2.185.
attribution_note: Guha (Nishadraj) to his men, agreeing with an old man of his clan.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Guha sees Bharat's army coming to the Ganga and assumes he means to kill Ram; he readies his men to die blocking the crossing. An old man reads a good omen and says Bharat may be coming for another reason. Guha agrees, tells his men to hold the ghats while he goes to learn whether Bharat is friend, foe or neutral, and then sets out with gifts to meet him.
core_teaching: Rash action without understanding the other person brings regret and damages one's own good. Find out someone's intent before treating them as an enemy.

commentaries.gist: Guha praises the old man because he is himself skilled at reading omens and the elder's years were spent in reflection.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, citing a Sanskrit subhashita
commentaries.gist: Hasty deeds ripen into consequences that hurt the heart like an embedded stake. Compares the sky-voice to Lakshman later (231.3-4), which makes the same point.
'Ghat gahahu' means gather and hold the river landing, keeping position while the facts are checked, not disbanding the guard.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to conflict at work or at home: check your assumptions about someone's motives before you act. Guha still keeps his guard posted; caution and openness go together.
misreadings: Not a call to drop all defences: Guha keeps the ghats guarded while he investigates.
speaks_to: anger that wants to act right now
not_for: someone facing a known, clear threat who needs to act fast

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 204 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 204). NOT 2.196: our id and label are off by eight.
attribution_note: Bharat to Triveni (the river confluence at Prayag), asking for a boon.
translation_note: Accurate. 'gati nirbana' is liberation (moksha). 'ruci' is relish or desire.
context: Bharat reaches Prayag on his way to Chitrakoot and asks the Triveni for alms, setting aside his kshatriya pride. He asks for none of the four aims of life, only love for Ram's feet in every birth. In the following lines he adds: let Ram think me crooked and people call me a traitor to guru and master, as long as my love keeps growing, like the chataka bird whose love for the cloud only grows when the cloud ignores it, or gold that shines brighter in fire.

key_terms.sense: not wealth, not duty, not pleasure (three of the four aims)
love for Ram's feet birth after birth

core_teaching: Bharat asks only for love itself, and for it in every life, rather than for any reward, even liberation. In the lines that follow he wants that love whether or not it is returned or praised.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He refuses all four aims up front so they won't be offered instead. Rebirth is welcome if every birth has this love, a one-sided love that doesn't depend on Ram being pleased.

commentaries.who: Ayodhya Dipika (A. Di.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Reads 'birth after birth' as a wish to be born wherever Ram is, so that the love stays and nothing without Ram counts.

commentaries.who: Pt. Yadavshankar Jamdar, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: For Bharat love of Ram's feet is both the means and the goal: there is no separate prize beyond the love, so there is no room for dissatisfaction.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to describe loving something for itself, not for its returns: the devotion is the reward. It can also mark the difference between serving to be noticed and serving because you love.
misreadings: Not a rejection of duty or earning a living: Bharat is a prince who goes on to govern.
Not a sectarian claim that liberation is worthless; it voices the bhakti preference for love over release.
cautions: Rebirth doctrine is assumed.
speaks_to: someone whose motives in service have become mixed
not_for: someone who needs practical help with money or work right now

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 205, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 205.7-8). NOT 2.197.
attribution_note: A voice from the middle of the Triveni. Pt. Ramkumar in Manas Piyush says the voice is Saraswati, who flows in the middle of the confluence. 'Triveni (a voice from the rivers)' is fine; could add 'Saraswati'.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Bharat has just asked Triveni for love of Ram in every birth, even if Ram thinks him crooked and the world calls him a traitor. A soft, auspicious voice rises from the middle of the confluence with this answer. Bharat thrills, the gods shower flowers, and the people of Prayag talk of his pure love; he then goes on to the sage Bharadwaj.

key_terms.sense: good in every way (thought, word and deed)

key_terms.term: तुम्ह सम रामहि कोउ प्रिय नाहीं
key_terms.sense: no one is as dear to Ram as you

core_teaching: The voice removes Bharat's guilt point by point: he is not crooked but good, his love is boundless, and the love is returned more than he imagines.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Majh Triveni' is apt because Saraswati is in the middle of the confluence; she is the speaker. 'Agadhu': no one, not guru, Guha, Lakshman, Janaka or the gods, could find the bottom of his love.
Bharat's guilt was the charge of crookedness and treachery he laid on himself. 'Good in every way' answers that, and 'none dearer to Ram' answers his fear that Ram would reject him.
By telling him he already has all he asked for, Saraswati shows there is nothing more anyone could give him.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for people who punish themselves for things they didn't do: sometimes the most useful thing is for someone to say plainly that the guilt is misplaced and that they are loved.
misreadings: Not a statement that guilt is always pointless; it addresses guilt for something one didn't do.
speaks_to: fear that someone you love has turned against you
needing reassurance after a family rupture
not_for: someone who has really done harm and needs to make amends first

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 206 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 206). NOT 2.198.
attribution_note: The sage Bharadwaj to Bharat at Prayag.
translation_note: Accurate. 'gai gira mati dhuti': Saraswati (gira, the goddess of speech) deceived or swept away her mind.
context: Bharat sits before Bharadwaj, head bowed, dreading questions. The sage speaks first: we have heard everything; no one can resist Providence. Then this doha. He goes on to say that even if Bharat had taken the throne he would have done no wrong, that Kaikeyi acted under destiny and repented, and that anyone who calls Bharat guilty is base.
core_teaching: Bharat should not carry shame for his mother's act, and even she is not to be blamed, because her mind was turned by a higher plan. The sage lifts the shame from both son and mother.

commentaries.gist: Bharadwaj declares Kaikeyi blameless in front of everyone so that Bharat's shame lifts and no one can blame him. What happens by destiny cannot be stopped.
Earlier the Manas says Saraswati turned Manthara's mind; here Kaikeyi's. Resolution: Saraswati turned Manthara, and through Manthara, Kaikeyi, so both can be credited to her.

commentaries.who: Ramayan Prakash (Ra. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Bharadwaj moves the blame step by step: first to Providence, then to Saraswati, then (as the world sees it) to Kaikeyi, and in the end to destiny itself.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to people ashamed of a parent's or relative's wrongdoing: you are not your family's mistakes. It also models refusing to scapegoat even the one who did the wrong.
misreadings: Not a claim that people are never responsible for what they do: it is a specific mythic framing of Kaikeyi's role in the divine plan.
Should not be used to tell a victim that their abuser 'couldn't help it'.
cautions: The 'a god clouded her mind' framing may sound like excusing harm to someone hurt by a relative.
speaks_to: shame over a parent's or sibling's actions
being judged for a relative's choices
not_for: someone currently being harmed by the family member in question

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 212, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 212.7-8). NOT 2.204.
attribution_note: First half is narration (the sages praise Bharat); second half is Bharadwaj to Bharat. Our speaker field is right for the quoted words.
translation_note: Accurate. 'sabahin' are the sages present; Manas Piyush's meaning says the munis were pleased and all praised him.
context: Bharat has told Bharadwaj that his only grief is that Ram suffers because of him. The sages are moved and praise him. Bharadwaj consoles him: don't grieve so much, all sorrow will end when you see Ram's feet. He then invites Bharat to be his guest, and goes on to host the whole army with his powers.
core_teaching: The sage gives Bharat a near, concrete hope: the pain will ease once he sees the one he longs for.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: This blesses Bharat's earlier words that the burning in his heart would not go until he saw Ram. It comes true: he finds relief even at the sight of Ram's footprints, and later in the sandals.
Bharadwaj, who knows all, does not bless him with Ram's return, since he knows Ram will not come back; he offers only comfort and says only what will happen.
Lists others in the Manas whose sorrow ends at the sight of Ram's feet: Guha, the forest people, Kabandha, Vibhishana, the boatman, Ahalya.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for the comfort of a reunion ahead: holding on to the next real step (seeing the person, making the call) can ease a grief that argument can't.
misreadings: Not a promise that everything will be fixed: Panjabi ji points out the sage carefully does not promise Ram's return.
speaks_to: longing to see someone you are estranged from
not_for: grief for someone who has died, where 'you'll see them' would be hollow

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 219, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 219.3-4). NOT 2.211.
attribution_note: Brihaspati to Indra, describing Ram's nature.
translation_note: Accurate. Note the very next line (219.3) qualifies it: even so, he deals evenly or unevenly according to whether a heart is devoted or not. A reading should not stop at 'as you sow'.
context: Indra fears that Bharat's love will bring Ram home and wreck the gods' plans, and wants to use illusion on Bharat. Brihaspati tells him to drop the trickery: harming Ram's devotee rebounds on the plotter. He describes Ram's nature: even-handed and untouched by anyone's merit or sin, he has made the world run on action, though he still responds to devotion. The next lines say Ram is angered by offences against his devotees.

key_terms.sense: with action as the governing principle

key_terms.term: जो जस करइ सो तस फलु चाखा
key_terms.sense: whoever does a thing tastes its fruit in kind

core_teaching: God is impartial and does not personally take on anyone's sins or merits; instead the world is ordered so that actions bear their own fruit. Brihaspati uses this to warn Indra that scheming against a good person will come back on him.

commentaries.gist: He takes on neither sin (left to Yama) nor merit (left to Brahma); beings reap joy or pain from their own deeds, so he stays untouched. Cites the Brahma Sutra on God's impartiality.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, citing Gita 5.15 with Ramanuja's bhashya
commentaries.gist: The all-pervading Self takes on no one's sin or merit; the sense of 'mine' and 'enemy' comes from ignorance covering knowledge.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, quoting Parashara and Bhishma (Mahabharata, Shanti Parva)
commentaries.gist: Sin is like dye that washing won't remove; deeds follow their doer like a shadow and bear fruit in their own time, knowingly done or not.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it as a reason to act cleanly and not plot against others: you will live with the results of what you do. It is about one's own conduct, not about judging other people's suffering.
misreadings: Not a judgement that people who suffer must have deserved it (our misuse note is right).
Not the whole picture in the Manas: the next line says Ram responds to devotion too, so it is not a cold mechanism.
cautions: 'You reap what you sow' can wound someone who is suffering through no fault of their own.
speaks_to: temptation to scheme or cut corners
not_for: someone suffering illness, loss or abuse who may hear it as blame

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 220, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 220.1-2). NOT 2.212.
attribution_note: Brihaspati to Indra.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Prabhu' here is Ram, who is 'satyasandh' (true to his vow) and the gods' benefactor; Bharat follows Ram's command.
context: This closes Brihaspati's counsel to Indra. Ram has promised the gods he will relieve the earth, so he will keep that vow; Bharat only follows Ram's wishes; Indra's agitation comes from his own self-interest. Hearing this Indra is relieved, showers flowers and starts praising Bharat.
core_teaching: Indra's fear of Bharat's goodness comes from his own self-interest; the fault lies in his confusion, not in Bharat. Seeing this clearly turns his anxiety into admiration.

commentaries.gist: Ram is true to his word, so he will keep his earlier promise to the gods to lift the earth's burden; he also reassured them at Chitrakoot. Indra has nothing to fear.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar and Panjabi ji (tippani 2), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Indra accepted the good counsel, so he is called 'best of gods'. His joy is relief: had he used illusion on Bharat he would have come to grief.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to look at envy and anxiety about someone else's success: often the threat is in our own interests, not in the other person. Naming that can turn rivalry into respect.
misreadings: Not a rule that all anxiety is selfish; it addresses fear of another person's goodness.
speaks_to: envy of a colleague or sibling
not_for: someone whose fear of another person is well founded (abuse, real threat)

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 231, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 231.3-4). NOT 2.222.
attribution_note: A voice from the sky (akashvani) to Lakshman. Manas Piyush notes the gods speak it when the world is gripped by fear at Lakshman's rage.
translation_note: Accurate. 'anuchit uchit kaju kichhu hou' can also be read 'whatever is to be done, to judge whether it is right or wrong'.
context: At Chitrakoot, Lakshman sees Bharat's army and is sure Bharat has come to attack; he speaks in fury and readies his bow, and the world trembles. A voice from the sky first praises Lakshman's might, then gives this counsel. Lakshman is abashed; Ram and Sita honour him and Ram explains that Bharat could never be corrupted by power.

key_terms.sense: the wise say they are not wise

core_teaching: Any action, right or wrong, should be done after understanding; acting rashly and regretting later is not wisdom. Here it checks a loyal man's anger before he strikes someone he has misjudged.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Placing 'wrong' first hints that Lakshman's plan is wrong; even a right deed earns praise only if done with thought. Cites the proverb that the hasty are foolish and the patient deep.

commentaries.who: Nange Paramhans ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Lakshman's readiness to fight for his master is right; only attacking without checking is a little wrong. The voice is mainly to stop him, like a lion pouncing first, not a general sermon.
Ram let Lakshman finish because it is rude to cut someone off and he wanted to know his whole mind; afterwards Ram and Sita honour him so his embarrassment eases.
A wise person weighs the outcome before acting; rash deeds ripen into pain that burns the heart like an arrow.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to anger and impulsive decisions: pause, check the facts, then act. Loyalty and passion are good, but they need understanding.
misreadings: Not a call to never act decisively; it asks for thought first, not paralysis.
speaks_to: anger that wants to act now
jumping to conclusions about someone's motives
impulsive decisions at work or in family conflict
not_for: a genuine emergency that needs immediate action
research_note: DATA ERROR: our prasang is 'rcm.p.dasharath_promise' (Kaikeyi's two boons), which has nothing to do with this verse. It belongs with Lakshman's anger at Bharat's approach at Chitrakoot.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 234, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 234.1-2). NOT 2.225: our id and label are off by nine.
attribution_note: Bharat to himself, walking toward Chitrakoot.
translation_note: Accurate. 'panahi' is shoe or sandal. 'jau ... jau' is best read 'whether ... or'.
context: Bharat nears Ram's hermitage turning things over: Ram might take him to be party to his mother's plot, or might forgive him for his own goodness' sake. Here he concludes that either way his only refuge is Ram's sandals. The next line praises the chataka bird and the fish, famous for constant love; then Tulsidas describes him walking, slowed by shame and pulled by love.

key_terms.sense: Ram is a good master; all fault is the servant's

core_teaching: Whatever the outcome, rejection or honour, Bharat will keep his refuge in Ram. He takes all fault on himself and trusts the master's goodness.

commentaries.gist: Rejection is mentioned first because that is his fear; when he remembers Ram's nature comfort returns and he names the second possibility. Either way he has no other refuge.
Refuge in the sandals is fitting: a shoe is on the servant's head either way, as a blow if he is scorned or as an honour if he is accepted.
Tulsidas's own prayers voice the same stance: even if you abandon me I won't abandon you; like the chataka I keep my vow of love.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for steady loyalty that doesn't depend on being accepted: doing the right thing and leaving the response to the other. Also used for approaching someone you fear has judged you.
misreadings: Not a call to stay where you are rejected or harmed (our misuse note is right).
'All the fault is the servant's' is Bharat's humility, not a principle that the less powerful party is always to blame.
cautions: 'All fault is mine' can reinforce harmful self-blame in someone already blaming themselves.
speaks_to: fear of rejection before a reconciliation
faith that doesn't depend on outcomes
not_for: someone in an abusive relationship
someone with harsh self-blame

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 234, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 234.5-6). NOT 2.225.
attribution_note: Tulsidas narrating.
translation_note: Close. Manas Piyush reads 'bhagati bal dhiraj dhori' as devotion's strength and steadiness acting as the lead ox that pulls the cart; 'like a patient ox' is a fair compression.
context: Bharat walks on, body slack with shame and love. His mother's wrong seems to turn him back while devotion and steadiness pull him forward, and thinking of Ram's nature quickens his steps. The next lines compare him to a water-beetle in a current, darting and stalling, and say Guha forgot his own body watching him.

key_terms.sense: his mother's misdeed turning him back

core_teaching: Shame holds him back but remembering the other person's goodness moves him forward. Trust in someone's nature can outpull guilt.

commentaries.gist: 'Dhori' is the extra lead ox yoked in front when a cart is heavily loaded; devotion and steadiness are that extra pull under a heavy load of shame.
His body is slack from two things at once: shame about his mother's act and love from remembering Ram's nature.

commentaries.who: Vir Kavi, in Manas Piyush (on the next line)
commentaries.gist: The water-beetle image: in a stream it sometimes halts and then darts ahead, as Bharat's walk alternates between hesitation and haste.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to walking toward a hard conversation: guilt slows you, but focusing on the other person's goodness rather than your own failure helps you keep going.
speaks_to: mixed feelings of shame and love
not_for: someone wanting practical instructions

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 244, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 244.1-2). NOT 2.235: our id and label are off by nine.
attribution_note: Tulsidas narrating.
translation_note: Accurate. 'rukh rakhi' is 'honoured each one's wish/inclination'.
context: Bharat has met Ram, and now the whole company from Ayodhya reaches Chitrakoot, every person grieving and longing in their own way. Ram, with Lakshman, meets them all in a moment and eases their burning pain. Tulsidas adds that this is no great thing for Ram, just as one sun is reflected in millions of water pots. He then goes first to Kaikeyi.

key_terms.sense: honoured each one's wish in just that way

core_teaching: Ram meets each distressed person according to the relationship and longing they bring. Compassion, understanding and the power to act are all needed together.

commentaries.gist: Each epithet matters: compassion alone can't help without knowing what the sufferer needs (sujan), and knowing is useless without power (Bhagavan). Ram has all three, so he relieves them at once.
'Whatever feeling': as disciple, son, brother, friend, king; compares Bal Kand 241, where each person saw the Lord according to their own feeling.
He did not take many bodies, since he is in ascetic dress; each simply saw him as they wished, like one sun reflected in many pots.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to describe good care: meet each hurting person in the way they need, not with one script for all. Seeing what each person longs for is part of compassion.
speaks_to: caring for several grieving people at once
not_for: someone wanting a strict ethical rule

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 244, chaupai 4 plus doha 244 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 244.7-8 and doha 244). NOT 2.235. Our text runs one chaupai and the doha together.
attribution_note: Narration, with the doha's last line as Ram's words to the mothers.
translation_note: Close. 'saral subhayan bhagati mati bhei' means his simple nature and his mind soaked in devotion (to her as mother); it is Ram's mind that is soaked, not hers that he soothes. 'amb' (mother) in the doha is Ram addressing the queens.
context: At Chitrakoot Ram sees the mothers, wilted like vines struck by frost. He goes to Kaikeyi first, falls at her feet, and comforts her by laying the blame on time, karma and fate. Then he meets the other queens and tells them all that the world is in God's hands and no one should be blamed. He then greets the gurus' wives, Sumitra and Kausalya.

key_terms.sense: his mind soaked in devotion (to her as mother)

key_terms.term: काल करम बिधि सिर धरि खोरी
key_terms.sense: putting the blame on time, karma and fate

core_teaching: Ram goes first to the person who caused his exile and takes away her blame, then asks everyone else not to blame anyone. Forgiveness here is active: he puts the guilty one at ease.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi (Vi. Tri.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: All the mothers were grieving but Kaikeyi most, knowing she caused it, so Ram met her first with no trace of resentment; when the others began to blame her he told them the world is in God's hands.
'Simple nature': Ram had always treated Kaikeyi as mother. 'Time, karma, fate' name three ways of explaining what happened, and the timing of the boon shows each at work.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 3), in Manas Piyush, citing Gita 18.61
commentaries.gist: The final word is that the Lord who dwells in all hearts moves everything; time and karma are only names. Some read Ram as hinting he took the blame himself.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to family ruptures: go first to the one who hurt you and help them carry their remorse, and discourage the rest of the family from piling on blame.
misreadings: Not pretending the harm didn't happen (our misuse note is right).
Not a demand that a victim must comfort the person who hurt them; Ram chooses to.
cautions: 'Blame no one' may feel like erasure to someone still being harmed.
not_for: someone in an ongoing abusive situation
someone not ready to forgive

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 258, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 258.1-2). NOT 2.247: our id and label are off by eleven.
attribution_note: First half Vasishtha to Ram; second half Ram's reply. Our setting says this.
translation_note: Accurate. 'aarat' is the distressed, those in pain. Vaijnath (in Manas Piyush) reads the first half as Vasishtha saying he won't give the order because he too is distressed.
context: At the Chitrakoot assembly Vasishtha says to Ram: you know every heart; tell us the course that is good for the people, the mothers and Bharat. Then he adds this line to explain why he doesn't decide himself. Ram replies that the remedy is in the guru's hands and he will obey whatever he says.

key_terms.sense: a gambler sees only his own throw
master, the remedy is in your hands

core_teaching: People in pain cannot weigh things fairly; like a gambler they see only their own stake. So Vasishtha counts himself among them and hands the decision to Ram, and Ram hands it back.

commentaries.gist: In distress the power to judge goes; the sufferer says whatever seems to bring relief. Compares Vinaya Patrika 34, where the very distressed are not to be blamed for speaking without thought.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The throw that fell is really Ram's (the exile is his dharma), but everyone shouts for their own wish that he come home, as gamblers do.
Vasishtha means: I will not give an order, because I am one of the distressed.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a reason to delay big decisions in the middle of grief or crisis, and to ask someone steadier to help weigh things.
misreadings: Not a reason to dismiss people who are hurting (our misuse note is right): Vasishtha includes himself.
not_for: someone who needs their distress taken seriously right now

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 260, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 260.7-8). NOT 2.249.
attribution_note: Bharat to the assembly at Chitrakoot.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Asked by Vasishtha and Ram to speak, Bharat says the guru has already said all he could. He recalls his master's nature: he never got angry even at an offender, and from childhood never broke Bharat's heart, even letting him win games he had lost. Then he turns to his own failings and says he has never been able to face Ram out of love and shyness.

key_terms.sense: made me win even when I lost the game

core_teaching: Bharat grounds his trust in Ram in small, concrete memories: years of kindness, including letting a little brother win. Those memories are why he dares to hope now.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Constant company often breeds disrespect, yet in all those years Ram never once slighted him.
Raises the objection that Bharat was away for years (Ram went with Vishvamitra; Bharat went to his uncle's), and answers that Bharat did not leave by choice.

commentaries.who: Manas Mayank and Pandey/Vaijnath, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Let me win though I lost' carries a plea: I have lost because of my mother's deed; let me win again now.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to show how trust is built in small moments, and how remembering someone's past kindness can give courage to approach them after a rift.
speaks_to: parents thinking about how they treat younger children
not_for: someone whose sibling relationship was hurtful (could sting)

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 263, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 263.5-6). NOT 2.252.
attribution_note: Ram to Bharat.
translation_note: Accurate. 'punyasilok' are people of holy renown.
context: Bharat has spoken of the suffering mothers and people and blamed himself. Ram answers: your shame is in vain, a being's course depends on God; in my view all the holy of every time and world rank below you. He goes on: even thinking ill of you ruins this world and the next; those who blame your mother have not sat with gurus and saints; remembering your name will wipe out sin.

key_terms.sense: a soul's course depends on God
the three times and three worlds

core_teaching: Ram removes Bharat's guilt by placing outcomes with God and then lifting him up: no one of holy fame anywhere ranks above him.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: This answers Bharat's distress at the suffering mothers and people: grieving that you caused it is pointless, since what people suffer is under Providence and karma.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush, citing Valmiki Ramayana 2.22.22 and 2.105.15
commentaries.gist: Joy and sorrow, gain and loss, coming and going with no visible cause are the work of fate; a person does not move by his own will alone.
'The holy of three times are below you' means no one so pure has been, is, or will be.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to answer someone drowning in guilt for others' suffering: what happened is bigger than them, and the people who love them see their worth clearly.
misreadings: Not a statement that people have no agency; it lifts needless guilt.
cautions: 'A soul's course depends on God' can sound fatalistic to someone grieving.
speaks_to: feeling responsible for a family crisis
needing to hear you are valued
not_for: someone who needs to take responsibility for a real wrong

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 264, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 264.1-2). NOT 2.253: our id and label are off by eleven.
attribution_note: Ram to Bharat.
translation_note: Close. 'kutarak' is wrong or perverse reasoning (arguing against yourself), slightly stronger than 'needless doubts'. Pandeyji in Manas Piyush gives a second sense of the first line: the earth is sustained by Bharat, as his name ('one who sustains') suggests.
context: Continuing his reply to Bharat's self-blame, Ram swears by Shiva that the earth stands by Bharat's keeping. He tells him not to argue against himself, since love and hostility cannot be hidden. He then proves it: birds and beasts go near sages but flee from hunters, so if even animals know friend from foe, how could humans not know Bharat's love?

key_terms.sense: the earth stays because you keep it
enmity and love can't be hidden however you hide them

core_teaching: Ram tells Bharat to stop building arguments against himself: love shows itself, and everyone, Ram included, can see Bharat's.

commentaries.gist: Vasishtha, Bharat and Ram each swear by Shiva in this assembly to vouch for their truthfulness.
Two readings: the earth's protection is in Bharat's hands because Ram has promised to do what he says; or the earth is sustained by Bharat, as his very name means 'one who sustains'.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: This answers Bharat's own words that the sage and Ram know whether his love is true. If even animals tell friend from foe, so can humans; and Ram would have moved away had he doubted Bharat.

commentaries.who: Nange Paramhans ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The two examples, birds and deer, stand for Sita and Ram: both of them know Bharat wishes them well.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for people who keep arguing themselves into guilt despite clear evidence of their good intent: your love is visible to those who matter; stop prosecuting yourself.
misreadings: Not a claim that hidden malice is impossible to disguise in every case; it reassures Bharat.
speaks_to: fearing that someone doubts your love
not_for: someone being gaslit, who needs to trust their own perception of another's hostility (could cut either way)

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 267, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 267.3-4). NOT 2.256: our id and label are off by eleven.
attribution_note: Bharat to Ram.
translation_note: Accurate. Note the sentence is completed by the next line (267.3): all these together dug in to ruin me, but the protector of those who bow kept his vow. Our translation ends with an ellipsis; a reading should include that resolution.
context: Vasishtha has been pleased and Ram has reassured him, so Bharat says the false pain in his mind is gone. He admits he was afraid of a fear of his own making: the sun is not at fault if someone loses their sense of direction. He lists the real causes (his bad luck, his mother's crookedness, hard fate, hard times) and then says Ram, protector of the surrendered, kept his vow anyway.

key_terms.sense: a worry with a real root (here denied)

key_terms.term: रबिहि न दोसु देव दिसि भूलें
key_terms.sense: it's not the sun's fault, lord, if one loses direction

core_teaching: Bharat recognises that his dread of rejection was his own confusion, not anything in Ram. The real troubles were circumstance; the relationship itself was never at risk.

commentaries.gist: The 'root' of fear would be Ram, and there was none on his side. The sun always rises in the east; if someone thinks it rose in the west, the error is theirs. Cites Uttar Kand 73.
Explains the four causes: misfortune that brought separation, his mother's stubbornness, his own past karma ripening, and the hard times, likened to an evil star rising.
All four causes repeat things Bharat said in his earlier speech, where he blamed his luck, his mother, fate and the times.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to name 'apdar', fear we manufacture ourselves. Much of our dread about how someone sees us is our own confusion, like losing one's sense of direction and blaming the sun.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of real hardship: Bharat still names the real causes.
speaks_to: relief after a feared conversation went well
not_for: someone whose fear is well-founded

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 283, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 283.5-6). NOT 2.271: our id and label are off by twelve.
attribution_note: Kausalya to Sunayana (Janaka's queen) and the other queens at Chitrakoot.
translation_note: Accurate. 'samay subhaye' is read by Manas Piyush as 'by time (a hard time) and by nature, naturally'.
context: At Chitrakoot Janaka's queen visits Kausalya. Kausalya says even Saraswati can't describe Bharat's virtues, any more than one can bail out the sea with a shell. She has always known Bharat to be the lamp of the family, as the king told her again and again; gold and gems are tested, and so are people, by time. Then she checks herself: it is not right to say this today, grief and love reduce one's prudence.

key_terms.sense: gold tested by rubbing (on the touchstone)
a gem when it reaches the jeweller

core_teaching: Character is proven by difficult times, as gold by the touchstone. Bharat's behaviour in crisis has confirmed what his father always said about him.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The king kept telling her Bharat was the family's lamp; she did not fully believe it then, and now she has seen it was true.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar, in Manas Piyush, citing a subhashita
commentaries.gist: Gold is tested four ways (rubbing, cutting, heating, beating); a person is tested by generosity, conduct, virtue and action.
A person is truly good when their nature stays the same in good times and bad; Bharat stayed steady in the worst of times.
She checks herself because praising Bharat now could seem to push against what he came for, giving up a kingdom to bring Ram back.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that hard times reveal who people are, including ourselves; how someone acts under pressure tells you more than their words in calm times.
misreadings: Not a call to deliberately 'test' people with hardship.
speaks_to: seeing someone's true character in a crisis
being judged by how you handled hard times
not_for: someone who feels they 'failed the test' in a crisis and is ashamed

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 293, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 293.7-8). NOT 2.280: our id and label are off by thirteen.
attribution_note: Bharat to Janaka.
translation_note: Mostly. 'bair andh premahi na prabodhu' is read two ways in Manas Piyush: 'enmity is blind and love lacks understanding', or 'love is blind (and deaf) and cannot be reasoned with'. Our 'hatred is blind, and love has no judgement' follows the first; fine.
context: Janaka's party has arrived and Janaka asks Bharat what should be done. Bharat says he is a servant, the duty of service is notoriously hard, a master's duty and self-interest conflict, and love clouds judgement. In the doha that follows he asks the elders to decide, keeping Ram's wish, dharma and vow in view, treating him as one who is not free, and recognising everyone's love.

key_terms.sense: the duty of service is hard
duty to the master opposes self-interest
love cannot see clearly / cannot be reasoned with

core_teaching: Bharat declines to judge his own case: a servant's duty is hard, his own interest pulls against it, and love blinds as surely as hatred does. So he asks others to decide with everyone's good in view.

commentaries.gist: Keeping Ram's wish, dharma and vow is the servant's duty; wanting everyone's good and love is a kind of self-interest. The two conflict, so deciding is hard.
Bharat means: I think myself guilty while Ram praises my love; either way my judgement is compromised, so you decide. The words are so deep that Tulsidas next calls them 'most wonderful speech'.
Paraphrases the request as: keep to Ram's dharma and vow, treat me as dependent, and do what all agree is good for all.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to explain recusing yourself from a decision you're too close to: love, like anger, distorts judgement, and naming that is wisdom, not weakness.
misreadings: Not a claim that love is bad or that loyalty is foolish.
speaks_to: serving others when your own wishes pull another way
not_for: someone who needs to trust their own judgement and is being told not to

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 294, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 294.1-2). NOT 2.281.
attribution_note: Narration: Janaka (the 'Rau') and his court praise Bharat.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Bharat has just answered Janaka in a few words, asking the elders to decide by Ram's wish and everyone's good. Janaka and his court praise both his words and his nature. Tulsidas adds that the speech is like a face in a hand mirror: you hold the mirror but can't grasp the face. The whole party then goes to Ram.

key_terms.sense: boundless meaning in very few syllables

core_teaching: Good speech can be simple to hear yet deep, gentle yet firm, brief yet full of meaning. Bharat's reply is held up as such speech.

commentaries.gist: Easy to say, soft to hear, hard to understand fully; its sense is clear, yet it is firm toward others.
Maps each adjective onto Bharat's doha: keeping Ram's wish is easy, keeping dharma hard, 'I am dependent' gentle, 'by all's consent' lovely, 'all's good' firm (hard).
Disagrees on details: 'recognise love' is the firm part, a quiet hint that Janaka, called bodiless (Videha), may not grasp love between brothers.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi (Vi. Tri.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The mirror image explains 'few syllables, boundless meaning': the words are small and easily held, but their meaning can't be grasped whole.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a model for speaking in conflict: few words, kind and firm at once, saying more by saying less.
not_for: someone looking for emotional comfort

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 298, chaupais 1-4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 298.1-8, half-lines numbered separately). NOT 2.285, and our text is four chaupais, not one. Manas Piyush prints the start as 'prabhu pitu matu suhrid gur swami' as we do.
attribution_note: Bharat to Ram before the assembly.
translation_note: Accurate. The last line is read in Manas Piyush as: no master is like my master, and, I swear by him, no one (in baseness and offence against the master) is like me.
context: After Ram tells the assembly he will do what Bharat says, Bharat rises to speak. He opens with twenty epithets of Ram (father, mother, friend, guru, master, worthy, highest good, knower of hearts, simple, good master, ocean of good conduct, protector of those who bow, all-knowing, wise, mighty, friend of the surrendered, prizer of virtues, remover of faults) and then sets himself as the opposite. He goes on to confess that he came against orders.

key_terms.sense: protector of those who bow down
the good of those who take refuge

core_teaching: Bharat names every way Ram is the perfect refuge, and in contrast calls himself the worst servant. The praise prepares the ground for his confession and request.

commentaries.gist: Twenty epithets in three lines. 'Prabhu' signals power to do even the impossible, here to keep his father's, the guru's and Janaka's words all at once. 'Father, mother': he sustains and pampers like parents.
Simple: though so great he is easy to reach, rising to embrace a boatman. Good master: ordinary masters get angry on hearing of a servant's fault; Ram overlooks faults he has seen.

commentaries.who: Vaijnath (Vai.), citing Bhagavad-guna-darpana, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Defines 'shil' (good conduct) as the great mixing without reserve with the lowly, poor, impure and despised.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a prayer of trust, a list of what one hopes for in a parent, mentor or God, and as a model of humility before asking for something important.
misreadings: Not a reason to see oneself as worthless: 'no one like me' is devotional humility.
cautions: The self-abasing last line can reinforce low self-worth if read alone.
speaks_to: gratitude to a mentor or parent
coming to someone you rely on completely
not_for: someone with harsh self-criticism (the last line)
research_note: Our text spans 298.1-4; the label says chaupai 1 only.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 298 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 298). NOT 2.285.
attribution_note: Bharat to Ram.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Bharat has just confessed that, out of delusion, he overrode the words of Ram and his father and came with the whole company; no one, high or low, ever set aside Ram's command even in thought, and he did. Yet Ram took the boldness as love and service. In this doha he says Ram's own kindness turned his faults into ornaments. He continues with Ram's ways with those who come for refuge.

key_terms.sense: by your own grace and goodness

core_teaching: Bharat credits Ram's goodness, not his own, with turning his offence into something honoured. Grace can transform even our mistakes.

commentaries.gist: Everyone's good comes from Ram's own goodness; compares Vinaya Patrika 152, which lists all whom Ram's goodness helped, from Ahalya to Vibhishana to the simple people of Ayodhya.
The 'fair fame' is that Bharat is now known as a great lover and saint who gave up a kingdom for Ram.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for gratitude when someone's generosity turned your mistake into something good, and for the hope that failures can become part of a good story.
misreadings: Not a license to do wrong and expect it to be turned to good.
speaks_to: a mistake that turned out well
a mentor who covered for you kindly
not_for: someone who has not been forgiven and is still hurting

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 299, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 299.3-4). NOT 2.286.
attribution_note: Bharat to Ram.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Teu' (even such people) refers to the list in the previous line: the cruel, crooked, wicked, ill-minded, disgraced, low, ill-mannered, masterless (or godless) and shameless.
context: Bharat describes Ram's way, famous in the world and sung by scripture: even the worst sorts of people, if they come to him for refuge, he takes as his own at a single bow; he sees their faults but never holds them in his heart, and praises their virtues among the good. He goes on: what master so honours a servant? Ram never even thinks of his own kindness, only of the servant's embarrassment.

key_terms.sense: came face to face, for refuge

key_terms.term: देखि दोष कबहुँ न उर आने
key_terms.sense: seeing faults, never kept them in his heart

core_teaching: Ram accepts anyone who turns to him, at once, without holding their past against them, and he publicly praises whatever is good in them.

commentaries.gist: 'Nirisa' means masterless, or one with no God in his understanding (an atheist); 'nisanki' means one who does wrong without fear or shame.
Ordinary masters turn angry on hearing a servant's fault; Ram does not hold even faults he has seen, as the Manas says elsewhere.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a picture of generous leadership and friendship: don't keep score of people's faults, and speak about their good qualities in public.
misreadings: Not a claim that faults don't matter; it is about acceptance after turning back.
speaks_to: someone with a past they're ashamed of
leaders and parents learning to forgive
not_for: someone hurt by a person who is being 'accepted' without accountability
research_note: Manas Piyush gives only word notes and meaning for this exact line; the second commentary is the note on the nearby list of Ram's qualities (298), which makes the same point.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 300, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 300.1-2). NOT 2.287.
attribution_note: Bharat to Ram.
translation_note: Mostly. 'Rajayasu' is a royal command. Manas Piyush links this to 298.5, where Bharat says he overrode 'the Lord's and father's words', and notes the word hints that Ram is the true king. Our translation says 'against your will' and our setting says 'his father's order'; better to say 'setting aside the royal command (of Ram and his father)'.
context: Bharat is near the end of his confession. Whether from grief, love or childish stubbornness, he came setting the command aside; yet Ram, looking at his own nature rather than Bharat's fault, took it all as good. He goes on: I have seen your feet, known your natural kindness, and seen in this great gathering how much you love me despite my great mistake.

key_terms.sense: from grief, love, or a child's nature
looking to your own side (your own nature)

core_teaching: Bharat owns that he disobeyed, and marvels that Ram judged it by his own generous nature rather than by the offence.

commentaries.gist: Grief is the burning that drove him out; love is his wish to bring Ram back; 'a child's nature' is his stubbornness in ignoring guru, parents, ministers and even Ram's message.
'Looking to his own side': Ram does not look at a servant's offence but at his own kindness. Compares Bal Kand 28 and Vinaya Patrika 96-97.
In Valmiki too Ram tells Lakshman that Bharat has come only out of love and grief, for no other purpose.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to model honest confession that names mixed motives, and generous reception that judges people by their love rather than by the rule they broke.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of ignoring instructions; Bharat calls it a fault.
speaks_to: having acted impulsively out of love
being forgiven more kindly than expected
not_for: someone being told their disobedience to an abuser was wrong

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 304 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 304). NOT 2.290: our id and label are off by fourteen.
attribution_note: Ram to Bharat, before the gurus and the assembly.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Bharat has asked Ram to decide and command him. Ram begins his answer: Bharat, you are the upholder of dharma, wise in the world's ways and the Vedas, and skilled in love. Then this doha, after which he speaks of the solar dynasty's way, their father's truthfulness, and what each brother's duty now is: Ram's the forest, Bharat's the kingdom.

key_terms.sense: pure in deed, word and mind

core_teaching: Ram declares Bharat spotless in thought, word and deed, beyond comparison, while saying that propriety and the sad moment keep him from praising his younger brother more.

commentaries.gist: Speaking at length among elders is improper; praising a younger brother (who is like a son) to his face is against good manners; and in a time of grief no one can do justice to it anyway.
The same reticence appears when Vasishtha hesitates to praise Bharat to his face, and when Kausalya checks herself for praising him in a time of grief.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for affirming someone sincerely and specifically, while also knowing when public praise would be out of place.
speaks_to: needing to hear you are good
not_for: someone looking for advice on what to do
research_note: Our setting says Bharat 'blames himself for his mother's scheme' here; by doha 304 Bharat has finished his confession and asked Ram to decide. Minor.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 306, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 306.7-8). NOT 2.292.
attribution_note: Ram to Bharat.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Odiahin hath asanihu ke dhaye': the hands are raised to take even a thunderbolt's blow.
context: Ram has told Bharat that obeying father, mother, guru and master is the one practice that brings fame, a good end and prosperity, and that Bharat should bear the hardship and keep the people happy. Trouble has been shared out among all, but Bharat's share for the term will be hardest. Here Ram admits he is saying a hard thing to a tender person, justified by the bad time. The doha that follows compares servant and master to hands, feet, eyes and mouth.

key_terms.sense: even the blow of a thunderbolt

core_teaching: In a crisis it is right to ask the people closest to us to carry hard things, as the hand rises by instinct to shield the body from a blow.

commentaries.gist: 'Tender': Ram knows Bharat cannot bear separation. 'Hard': asking him to suffer and carry the kingdom. It is justified only because the time leaves no other way: the father is gone and both commands must be kept.
An example-and-image figure: the good brother is the hand, the bad time the thunderbolt. The hand rises first to shield the body even if it is hurt; outsiders don't stand by you in such moments.
Obeying parents protects reputation, obeying the guru brings a good end, and obeying the master (Ram) brings the power to stay near him.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for family responsibility in emergencies: the people who love us are asked to carry the heaviest loads, and asking them is honest, not cruel.
misreadings: Not a justification for always loading the 'soft' family member with burdens.
cautions: May sit badly with someone already carrying too much for their family.
speaks_to: being asked to step up in a family crisis
asking a loved one for something hard
not_for: a carer who is burned out and over-relied upon

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 307, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 307.7-8). NOT 2.293.
attribution_note: Bharat to Ram.
translation_note: Accurate. 'avalamb' is a support, something to lean on; 'avadhi paru pavaun' is to reach the far shore of the fixed term (the fourteen years).
context: Ram's words have settled the assembly and Bharat is content; his face clears, as if a mute had been given speech. He bows and says the joy of going with Ram and the fruit of his birth are his. Now he will carry out whatever Ram orders, but asks for a support to serve through the term. In the next lines he asks about the coronation gear and to see Chitrakoot's holy places; later Ram gives him his sandals.

key_terms.sense: placing it on my head (accepting with reverence)
crossing to the end of the term

core_teaching: Bharat accepts the hard command fully but asks for something concrete to hold on to through the long separation.

commentaries.gist: Ram had only spoken of parents' and guru's orders, not given his own; so here Bharat asks for an order from Ram himself and promises to obey at once.
He is ready to go but has three requests: a support to cross the sea of separation for fourteen years, instructions about the coronation materials, and leave to see Chitrakoot's holy sites.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to long separations and hard assignments: accept what must be done, and ask for something tangible (a keepsake, a routine, a practice) to carry you through.
speaks_to: needing a ritual or object to get through a long wait
not_for: someone who needs to be told they can refuse

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand doha 315 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 315). NOT 2.301: our id and label are off by fourteen.
attribution_note: Ram to Bharat. The name 'Tulsi' in the doha is the poet's signature; Manas Piyush reads it as Tulsidas reporting Ram's words.
translation_note: Accurate. 'sahit bibek' (with discernment) qualifies how the mouth nourishes the limbs: each according to its need.
context: In his parting counsel before Bharat returns to Ayodhya, Ram gives this image of the ruler. The next line says that this alone is the whole of rajadharma, like a wish held secretly in the mind. It echoes an earlier doha (306) where servants are hands, feet and eyes and the master the mouth.

key_terms.sense: sustains and nourishes all the limbs

core_teaching: A leader receives the resources, like the mouth receiving food, but only in order to distribute them wisely so every part of the body is nourished according to its need.

commentaries.gist: Read with doha 306: there servants are hands, feet and eyes bringing to the mouth; here the mouth's duty is named. 'With discernment' means giving each organ what it needs, neither more nor less, else disease follows.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: 'Discernment' covers place, time, season, friend, foe and neutral; the doha could be expanded into a whole treatise on statecraft, as Gita 6.17 on balanced living could.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi (Vi. Tri.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Society is a body and the leader its mouth; the next line's 'wish hidden in the mind' means this principle should drive all outward action.
This one doha contains all of rajadharma, as large wishes hide in a small mind.

practical_reading: Widely used in Indian management and civic teaching: leaders take in resources and credit, but their job is to distribute wisely and fairly, not to consume.
misreadings: Not a defence of leaders hoarding: the mouth eats only to feed the body.
speaks_to: anyone with power over shared resources
not_for: someone looking for personal emotional comfort

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kand 324, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 324.7-8). NOT 2.310.
attribution_note: Tulsidas narrating.
translation_note: Close, but misses the point of the bee image: commentators note bees are said not to settle on champak flowers, so a bee in a champak garden lives amid fragrance without tasting it. Also, Pt. Ramkumar reads the vomit simile as about other lovers of Ram and other wealth, not Bharat and Ayodhya's wealth, which belongs to Ram.
context: After returning, Bharat installs Ram's sandals and lives in a hut at Nandigram, fasting and in ascetic dress. Tulsidas says Ayodhya's wealth was the envy of Indra and Kubera, yet Bharat lived there without attachment. The doha that follows says this is no great feat for Bharat, the vessel of Ram's love, just as a chataka's constancy and a swan's discrimination are simply their nature.

key_terms.sense: a bee in a champak garden

core_teaching: Bharat lives surrounded by royal wealth without enjoying it, because it belongs to Ram; true lovers of Ram turn from luxury without effort.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ayodhya's wealth is Ram's, so calling it vomit would be wrong. Bharat gets the champak image (bees don't settle on champak); the vomit image is for other devotees and other wealth.

commentaries.who: Kharra (an old commentary), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The two images show renunciation inside and outside: 'living without attachment' is inner, 'giving up like vomit' is outward.
A servant should not enjoy his master's property; Bharat will take it only as prasad once Ram enjoys it, and Ram is now living on roots and fruit.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for living among comforts or power without being owned by them, and for holding resources in trust rather than as one's own.
misreadings: Not a call to despise money or family wealth; Bharat governs carefully.
The vomit simile is strong; it describes intense dispassion, not a rule for everyone.
cautions: The disgust image can feel harsh or shaming to someone struggling with money.
not_for: someone in financial hardship

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand soratha 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 2). Reference matches.
attribution_note: Narrative voice. In the Manas this section is told by Shiva to Bhavani (Parvati); Manas Piyush's meaning of the line just before begins '(Shiva says) Bhavani!'. 'Tulsidas -> the reader' is acceptable but 'Shiva to Parvati (narrator)' is more exact.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Chhoh' is tenderness, affection; 'droh' is treachery, hostile harm.
context: Jayant, Indra's son, took the form of a crow to test Ram's power, pecked Sita's foot and fled. Ram's grass-blade arrow chased him through all the worlds; no god would shelter him until Narada sent him back to Ram. When he cried out for protection, Ram let him go with one eye destroyed. This soratha closes the episode.

key_terms.sense: who is as merciful as Raghubir?

core_teaching: Ram tempers justice with mercy: the offender deserved death, but when he took refuge Ram spared him, leaving a lesser, fitting consequence.

commentaries.gist: Parvati may have doubted how blinding him in one eye counts as mercy, so Shiva answers at once: by right he should have died.
Mercy is named at the start, middle and end of the episode. Anger usually leaves no room for mercy (compares Parashurama), yet Ram, powerful and provoked, chose kindness.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (Pra. and note 2), citing Valmiki 5.38.35 and Adhyatma Ramayana
commentaries.gist: Taking one eye kept the arrow's word true and taught a lesson; it was the eye that saw and struck. Valmiki also says Ram spared him though he deserved death; Adhyatma says the eye was taken with his consent.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to show mercy and accountability together: the wrongdoer who turns back is spared the worst but still bears a consequence.
misreadings: Grace doesn't erase consequences (our misuse note is right): Jayant loses an eye.
Not a model for victims being expected to forgive their abuser.
cautions: Involves violence and maiming; the 'mercy' includes a punishment.
speaks_to: someone ashamed of a serious wrong who fears there is no way back
parents and managers deciding on discipline
not_for: a victim of harm who may hear it as pressure to forgive

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 10, chaupai 7 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 10.13-14). NOT 3.7: our id and label are off by three.
attribution_note: Narrative voice (Shiva to Bhavani in the Manas frame).
translation_note: Accurate.
context: The sage Sutikshna, hearing that Ram is coming, runs to meet him, lost in love: he forgets direction and who he is, goes forward and back, sings and dances. Ram hides behind a tree to watch. Seeing such love Ram appears inside his heart, and the sage sits motionless in the path, hair on end. Then Ram comes near and tries to wake him.

key_terms.sense: remover of the fear of worldly existence

core_teaching: Ram is moved by love so complete that he first watches unseen and then reveals himself within the devotee's heart, before meeting him outwardly.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (Pu. Ra. Ku.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He hides so as not to break the spell; if the sage saw him he would stop dancing. Notes Ram hides three times in the Manas: behind a vine, a tree and a bush.

commentaries.who: Panjabi ji, with Prajnananand Saraswati, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Like a father secretly watching his child play; but a mother cannot watch such a child for long, so his tenderness overflowed and he appeared in the sage's heart.
Laughing, weeping, singing and dancing without shame are marks of the highest devotee, who purifies the world.

commentaries.who: Manas Piyush (note on the ten states of love)
commentaries.gist: Sutikshna passes through nine of the classic ten states of love, from longing to stupor; Ram hides partly so the shock of meeting does not push him to the tenth.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that being lost in love or joy, even looking foolish, is not something to be ashamed of, and that sincere longing is itself seen and answered.
misreadings: Not a recommendation to lose touch with reality; it describes ecstatic devotion.
speaks_to: longing to be seen by God or a loved one
not_for: someone whose emotional overwhelm is distressing rather than joyful

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 16, chaupai 6 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 16.11-12). NOT 3.13: our id and label are off by three.
attribution_note: Ram to Lakshman, at Panchavati.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Kam adi mad dambh' is desire and the rest (anger, greed), pride and hypocrisy.
context: At Panchavati Lakshman asks Ram about knowledge, dispassion, maya and devotion. Ram teaches him, ending with the marks of bhakti: love for the saints' feet, regarding guru, parents and kin as Ram, and then this description of the devotee whose body thrills as he sings. The doha that follows completes it.

key_terms.sense: desire and the rest, pride, pretence
I am always in their power

core_teaching: Ram says he is held by the devotee whose love shows in body, voice and tears and who is free of desire, pride and pretence. The outward signs count only with the inner purity.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Thrill, choked voice and tears are three of the eight 'sattvic' signs of devotional emotion. Cites Rupa Gosvami's Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu on how they arise.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi (Vi. Tri.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Singing out of desire, pride in one's art, greed for reward or to be called devout may bring some benefit, but it is not loving devotion and cannot win the Lord.
'Always in their power': compares other Manas lines where Ram says he guards such devotees and dwells in them as wealth in a miser's heart.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to separate real devotion from performance: feeling that wells up is valued only when it is free of ego, greed and show.
misreadings: Not a test that you must cry or tremble to be devout; the point is freedom from pride and pretence.
speaks_to: worry that one's practice is hollow
not_for: someone who feels spiritually 'dry' and may read it as exclusion

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand doha 16 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 16). NOT 3.13.
attribution_note: Ram to Lakshman.
translation_note: Accurate. 'gati' is refuge or goal; 'bishram' is rest, repose.
context: This doha closes Ram's teaching on bhakti to Lakshman at Panchavati. Lakshman bows at his feet in joy, and some days pass in talk of dispassion, knowledge and right conduct before Shurpanakha arrives.
core_teaching: Those who rely on Ram alone in speech, action and thought and worship without wanting anything back are where he rests. 'Rest' implies being at home, not just present.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
