commentaries.gist: God dwells in every heart (Gita 18.61) but unmanifest; only in such hearts does he 'rest', since others keep demanding sons, wealth and fame or quarrel among themselves. Calls 'rest' a careful word choice.
Speech should tell only of God, actions be done for his pleasure, and the mind dwell on him; desire even for heaven or liberation should be absent.
'Rest' marks this as Ram's own home, linking to Valmiki's 'jahi na chahia' (Ayodhya 131), where the desireless heart is Ram's own house.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that the divine is most at ease in a person who isn't bargaining: wholehearted, undivided, wanting nothing back.
misreadings: Not a statement that God is absent from people who pray for help; commentators say he dwells in all hearts.
not_for: someone in acute need who must ask for help
research_note: Links directly to rcm.2.127.doha.1 (Ayodhya 131) in theme; a plan could pair them.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand doha 30 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 30). NOT 3.26: our id and label are off by four.
attribution_note: Narrative voice (Shiva to Parvati in the Manas frame).
translation_note: Accurate. Manas Piyush records a textual and syntactic debate about the line before (whether it is Jatayu remembering Ram's footprints, or Ram seeing Jatayu), which does not affect this doha.
context: Ram, searching for Sita, finds Jatayu lying wounded after fighting Ravana, remembering Ram's feet. Ram strokes his head and the vulture's pain is gone. Jatayu then tells him Ravana took Sita south, refuses Ram's offer to keep him alive, and dies in Ram's presence.

key_terms.sense: a face that is the home of beauty

core_teaching: Ram's touch and the sight of his face take away all of Jatayu's pain, though he is dying. Both the Lord's touch and the devotee's gaze are named as healing.

commentaries.gist: The touch comes from Ram's side, the gazing from the devotee's; both end in 'all pain gone'. Either one is enough to remove a devotee's suffering. Lists parallel touches (Sugriva, Hanuman, Bhushundi).
What vanished is the pain of the wounds Ravana gave; the grief for Sita still aches, which is why Jatayu next speaks sorrowfully of her abduction.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram asks him nothing first; the lesson drawn is that one should not question a dying person before easing them.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for the comfort of presence at the end of life: touch and a loved face can ease what words can't.
misreadings: Not a claim that faith removes physical death or illness; Jatayu still dies.
cautions: Deathbed scene. Gentle, but may be hard for someone recently bereaved or facing a loved one's death.
speaks_to: sitting with a dying loved one
not_for: someone whose loved one died alone (may sharpen guilt)

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 31, chaupai 5 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 31.9-10). NOT 3.27: our id and label are off by four.
attribution_note: Ram to Jatayu.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Jatayu has declined Ram's offer to keep his body alive. With tears in his eyes Ram tells him he has won a good end by his own deeds, that nothing is out of reach for those devoted to others' good, and sends him to his abode. He also asks Jatayu not to tell Dasharath about Sita's abduction; Ravana will tell him himself. Jatayu takes a divine form, praises Ram, and departs.

key_terms.sense: nothing in the world is hard to attain
one whose wishes are all fulfilled

core_teaching: Living for others' good makes every aim reachable, including liberation. Ram honours Jatayu's self-sacrifice by sending him to his own abode.

commentaries.gist: Serving others brings all four aims: the 'good end' is moksha, and 'nothing is hard' covers wealth, dharma and desire in this world.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: True service of others is impossible while one wants something for oneself, here or hereafter; selfless service is the saint's nature.
Such liberated servers can even return to the world at will to help others; leaving this worn-out, painful body is good.
'What can I give you?' shows Ram's generosity: having given everything, he still speaks as if he had nothing to offer.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to honour people who gave themselves for others, and to say that a life of service is itself complete.
misreadings: Not a promise of worldly success for altruists; it is spoken to a dying hero.
cautions: Deathbed and 'leave this body' language. Fine for honouring someone's sacrifice; risky for anyone with suicidal feelings or in fresh grief.
speaks_to: honouring a parent or mentor who sacrificed for others
not_for: someone with thoughts of self-harm ('leave this body')
fresh bereavement

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 33, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 33.1-2, where Shiva sums up the Jatayu episode). NOT 3.29: our id and label are off by four.
attribution_note: Shiva to Uma (Parvati), summing up. Our speaker 'Narrator' is fine; Manas Piyush identifies the voice as Shiva.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Amish bhogi' is meat-eater; 'jachat jogi' is what yogis beg for.
context: After Jatayu's death and Ram's performing his funeral rites, Shiva sums up for Parvati: Ram is tender-hearted and gracious without cause, giving a lowly flesh-eating bird the end yogis pray for. He adds that those who leave Hari for worldly pleasures are unfortunate.
core_teaching: Ram's grace does not depend on rank or merit: he gave the humblest creature the highest goal.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram's heart melts most at the suffering of the 'deen', meaning people who feel they have no spiritual means of their own, even if they practise.
Tender-hearted, so he wept at Jatayu's pain; kind to the lowly, so he gave liberation and did the funeral rites himself. Others are kind for a reason; Ram without one.
Objection: Jatayu gave his life for Sita, so how is the grace 'without reason'? Answer: even his strength and courage were Ram's gift (Gita 7.8-11).

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that grace isn't earned by status or purity; it reaches the lowest and most unlikely.
misreadings: Not a statement that animals or meat-eaters are worthless; 'lowly' sets up the contrast with the yogi's goal.
cautions: Pt. Ramkumar's note condemns meat-eating; a reader may find that judgemental.
not_for: someone looking for a death-free reading (the setting is a funeral)

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 35, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 35.3-4). NOT 3.31: our id and label are off by four.
attribution_note: First half Shabari to Ram; second half Ram to Shabari. Our speaker field 'Shabari and Ram' is right.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Aghari' (enemy of sin) is an address to Ram, rendered 'Lord'. 'Bhamini' is a respectful address to a woman; Manas Piyush notes Ram uses for Shabari the same word he used for Sita.
context: Shabari, an old forest woman of low birth, has waited years for Ram. She washes his feet and feeds him, then stands with folded hands saying she cannot praise him: she is of low birth, dull, and among women, counted lowest of the low, the dullest. Ram answers that he recognises only the bond of devotion, and in the next lines says caste, family, dharma, wealth, strength, kin, virtue and cleverness without devotion are like a cloud without water. He then teaches her the nine forms of devotion.

key_terms.sense: I recognise only one relationship: devotion

core_teaching: Shabari voices the social hierarchy that ranks her lowest; Ram sets it aside entirely: the only bond he recognises is devotion.

commentaries.gist: She descends step by step: low caste, then lower than low, then as a woman lower still, then the dullest of women. The rhetorical figure is a 'chain of decline'.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Ram calls her 'bhamini', the word he used for Sita, not for bodily beauty: whoever has devotion is beautiful in his eyes. All other ties are born of illusion.

commentaries.who: Ranbahadur Singh, citing the Shandilya Sutra, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Experience shows devotion, not learning or birth, is what reaches God: Dhruva as a child, the hunter, Valmiki, Raidas, Namdev and others.
Because she named her caste first, Ram breaks that tie first when he lists what doesn't count.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that worth before God is not set by caste, gender, wealth or ability; love is the only credential.
misreadings: The first half is Shabari's harsh self-description, which Ram's reply overturns; never show it alone (our misuse note is right).
Not a teaching that women or lower castes are lesser; it records a hierarchy in order to reject it.
cautions: Contains caste and gender hierarchy language. Manas Piyush's own older notes (Kharra, Pt. Ramkumar) restate caste rankings; do not carry those into readings.
speaks_to: feeling unworthy because of background or gender
not_for: a reader hurt by caste or gender discrimination if the first half is shown without Ram's answer

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 36, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 36.3-4). NOT 3.32: our id and label are off by four.
attribution_note: Ram to Shabari.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Ram, having eaten Shabari's fruit, teaches her the nine forms of devotion (navadha bhakti): company of saints, love of his stories, service of the guru, singing his virtues, mantra repetition with firm faith, self-restraint and good conduct, then the seventh to ninth. He ends by saying whoever has even one is most dear to him, and Shabari has all. She then directs him to Pampa and Sugriva and gives up her body in yogic fire. These lines give the seventh and eighth forms.

key_terms.sense: seeing the world evenly, as full of me
counting the saints greater than me
never, even in a dream, looking at others' faults

core_teaching: The seventh form is seeing the divine everywhere and honouring good people above God himself; the eighth is contentment with what comes and refusing to dwell on others' faults.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 4), in Manas Piyush, citing Bhagavata 11.2.41
commentaries.gist: Seeing everything as Ram is the mark of his worshippers: earth, water, sky, beings and rivers are all his body, to be bowed to.
Saints are to be held above Ram because realised saints lead people to him, and because a father loves whoever loves his son more than whoever loves him.
Saints are greater because they stay untouched by the world like a lotus leaf in water.

practical_reading: Teachers use these two as daily practices: look for the good (or the sacred) in everyone, be content with what you have, and stop scanning others for faults.
misreadings: 'Not seeing faults' doesn't mean ignoring harm done to you or others; it is about a habit of fault-finding.
speaks_to: wanting a simple daily spiritual practice
not_for: someone in a harmful situation who needs to see the other person's faults clearly

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 36, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 36.5-6). NOT 3.32.
attribution_note: Ram to Shabari.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Harash na dina' is 'neither elated nor dejected'. The sentence completes in 36.4 ('that one is most dear to me').
context: Ram, having eaten Shabari's fruit, teaches her the nine forms of devotion (navadha bhakti): company of saints, love of his stories, service of the guru, singing his virtues, mantra repetition with firm faith, self-restraint and good conduct, then the seventh to ninth. He ends by saying whoever has even one is most dear to him, and Shabari has all. She then directs him to Pampa and Sugriva and gives up her body in yogic fire. This line gives the ninth form and begins the conclusion.

key_terms.sense: woman, man, or any being at all

core_teaching: The ninth form is simplicity and honesty with everyone, trusting God, and staying steady through gain and loss. Having even one of the nine is enough, whoever you are.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Guile comes from 'I and mine' and from not fully trusting God. Only when one takes whatever comes as the Lord's gift do elation and despair fall away.

Elation comes from gaining good things and dejection from losing them; once one has found Ram, the gain or loss of passing things stops moving one, as cash means little to one who has the philosopher's stone.
'Woman' is named first because Shabari had called herself lowest for being a woman.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for steadiness and honesty: be straightforward, don't manipulate, trust, and don't ride every high and low.
misreadings: 'Not dejected' is not a rule against sadness; it describes a steady trust underneath.
cautions: Someone in depression may hear 'neither elated nor downcast' as a demand.
speaks_to: wanting to be more honest and less calculating
feeling excluded from spirituality by gender or background
not_for: someone in clinical depression
research_note: Our text ends mid-sentence ('whoever has even one...'); it must be paired with rcm.3.32.chaupai.4, as our setting for that verse already notes.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 36, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 36.7-8). NOT 3.32.
attribution_note: Ram to Shabari.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Ram, having eaten Shabari's fruit, teaches her the nine forms of devotion (navadha bhakti): company of saints, love of his stories, service of the guru, singing his virtues, mantra repetition with firm faith, self-restraint and good conduct, then the seventh to ninth. He ends by saying whoever has even one is most dear to him, and Shabari has all. She then directs him to Pampa and Sugriva and gives up her body in yogic fire. This line closes the teaching.

key_terms.sense: every kind of devotion firm (in you)
the state hard even for hosts of yogis

core_teaching: Anyone with even one form of devotion is most dear to Ram, and Shabari, a forest woman of low birth, has them all firmly; the goal yogis strive for is hers today.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: The one dear to God is whoever drops every other hope and worships him; cites similar promises to the monkeys, to Guha and to Bhushundi (man, woman or any being).
Even one of the nine is rare and seldom firm; in her all nine are firm. Her devotion is why he came, and the fruit of seeing him is her own true state.
Adhyatma says the nine are means for anyone, woman, man or animal, practised in sequence; the Manas's 'even one' is far stronger.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that a person written off by society may be furthest ahead spiritually, and that one sincere practice is enough to begin.
misreadings: Not a ranking of devotees over yogis in general; it is said to honour Shabari.
speaks_to: encouragement to start with one practice
not_for: someone wanting a strict path or method

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand doha 38 (ka), the first of two dohas numbered 38 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush prints both under 38). NOT 3.34: our id and label are off by four.
attribution_note: Ram to Lakshman, in the spring forest on the way to Pampa.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Khal' is villain, wicked one; 'chhobh' is agitation, disturbance.
context: Separated from Sita, Ram walks through the spring forest and describes it to Lakshman as the army of Kama, the god of desire: trees as tents, birds as war-elephants, and so on. Those who stay steady before it have true renown. Then this doha names the three strongest foes. The second doha 38 gives their weapons: greed's are wanting and pretence, desire's is woman alone, anger's is harsh speech.

key_terms.sense: agitation in the blink of an eye

core_teaching: Desire, anger and greed can unsettle even the wisest mind in an instant. Knowing their strength is the first defence.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani), in Manas Piyush, citing Gita 2.62 and 3.37
commentaries.gist: The three are really one, desire, taking three forms: dwelling on objects breeds attachment, attachment desire, thwarted desire anger.
Example: Narada, a home of wisdom, fell to desire on seeing a princess, then to longing, then to anger when thwarted; no one in the world escapes all three.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi (Vi. Tri.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: These are the world's great enemies because they shake even sages who wish everyone well; one must know their strength to protect oneself.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan (Pan. Ra. Va. Sha.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Practical defence: check a craving as it arises, don't answer harsh words, and don't let lustful thoughts settle. Keeping their weapons in view lets one control them.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a humbling reminder that no level of learning or practice makes anyone immune to craving, temper and greed; vigilance, not pride, is the safeguard.
misreadings: Not a statement that feelings of desire or anger are sinful in themselves; it warns of their power to overturn judgement.
cautions: The doha right after it calls woman desire's only weapon. Don't pair them without context; that framing is offensive to many readers today.
not_for: a woman reader if paired with the next doha's 'woman is desire's weapon'

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 39, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 39.5-6). NOT 3.35: our id and label are off by four.
attribution_note: Shiva to Uma (Parvati). The second line is narration.
translation_note: Incomplete. Our text has two lines, but the translation renders only the first. The second line ('puni prabhu gae sarobar tira, pampa nama subhaga gambhira') says: then the Lord went to the shore of the lake called Pampa, lovely and deep. It starts the next scene and is not part of Shiva's teaching. Either drop it from our text or translate it.
context: Ram has been lamenting Sita and describing desire's army. Shiva explains to Parvati: Ram is beyond the gunas and knows all hearts; he showed the plight of the lovelorn to strengthen dispassion in the steady. Anger, lust, greed, pride and illusion all fall away by Ram's grace; the one the magician favours isn't fooled by the magic show. Then Shiva gives his own testimony. The narrative resumes at Pampa lake.

key_terms.sense: the whole world is a dream

core_teaching: Shiva states from his own experience that devotion to God is what is real and lasting, while the world is like a dream.

commentaries.gist: Lest calling Ram's play a magic show make it seem false, Shiva adds that worship is real and the world dreamlike. In a magic show the place is real, the show false; here the reverse.
'My own experience': other sages hold the world real, so Shiva speaks for himself. Kharra adds that in ritual and worship the world is treated as real, in knowledge as unreal.
He addresses 'Uma' because it was this very scene of Ram searching for Sita that once deluded her (as Sati).

practical_reading: Teachers use it to put worries in proportion: much of what grips us is passing like a dream, while devotion and what it grows in us endure.
misreadings: Not 'nothing in your life matters' (our misuse note is right); it names what lasts.
Not a denial that suffering is real to the sufferer.
cautions: 'The world is a dream' can feel dismissive to someone in grief or pain.
speaks_to: perspective when caught up in worldly worries
not_for: fresh grief
someone in acute distress whose pain should be taken seriously

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 42, chaupais 2-3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 42.3-6). NOT 3.38: our id and label are off by four, and our text runs two chaupais.
attribution_note: Ram to Narada, then (last line) narration introducing Narada's request.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: After Ram's lament by Pampa, Narada comes, praises him, and asks for one boon though Ram already knows his heart. Ram answers with this assurance. Narada asks that the name 'Ram' be greater than all the Lord's other names; Ram grants it. Then, seeing Ram pleased, Narada asks why Ram stopped his marriage long ago.

key_terms.sense: never let go of this trust, even by mistake

core_teaching: Ram tells Narada there is nothing he withholds from his own; Narada should never lose that trust, even if a past request seemed refused.

commentaries.gist: Ram states his own nature, as he does to Vibhishana in Sundar Kand: he keeps no veil between himself and his devotee; all he has is theirs.
Nothing is dear to Ram except his devotee. 'Never lose this trust' is said for a reason: Narada's earlier request in the Bal Kand was not granted, so his faith could waver.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Narada had also asked 'do what is good for me'; Ram did that instead of the literal request, which is why it seemed refused.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for trust after an apparent 'no': a loving parent or God may withhold the thing asked for while giving what is really good.
misreadings: Not a promise that every request will be granted literally; the very next scene explains a refusal.
not_for: someone in grief over an unanswered prayer, if read as 'you will get anything'

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 43, chaupais 2-3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 43.3-6). NOT 3.39: our id and label are off by four, and our text runs two chaupais.
attribution_note: First line Narada to Ram; then Ram to Narada.
translation_note: Close. 'Saharosa' is glossed in Manas Piyush as 'gladly'. 'Argai' means pulling it aside or quietly separating. Manas Piyush records a reading dispute: 'sisu bachchh' (little child) versus 'sisu bichchhu' (a child grabbing a scorpion), with editors split.
context: Narada asks why, when Ram's maya had deluded him, Ram did not let him marry (the Bal Kand story of Vishvamohini, where Narada was given a monkey's face and cursed Vishnu). Ram explains he guards those who rely on him alone as a mother guards a toddler. He goes on to contrast the wise (grown sons) with humble devotees (little children), and the doha calls desire, anger and the like the army of delusion.

key_terms.sense: as a mother guards her child

core_teaching: Ram stops what his devotee wants when it would harm him, as a mother pulls her toddler away from fire or a snake. The refusal is protection, not rejection.

commentaries.gist: Those who rely on Ram alone are guarded as a mother guards a small child: the moment it runs for fire or a snake, she snatches it away.
Prefers the reading 'bichchhu' (scorpion): first the general claim, then the example of a child grabbing a scorpion, fire or snake.

commentaries.who: Nange Paramhans ji, in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Also defends 'scorpion' from manuscript copies: scorpions are commoner in homes than snakes, as greed besets devotees more than lust or anger, and the Lord guards against it too.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to reframe a painful 'no' from life or God as possible protection, and to describe how good parents say no.
misreadings: Not a promise that nothing painful will happen (our misuse note is right).
Not a reason to stay passive or refuse medical, legal or emotional help.
cautions: Telling someone their loss was 'for their protection' can wound; use only for a reader reflecting on their own past.
speaks_to: a relationship that didn't work out, seen in hindsight
not_for: fresh loss or bereavement
abuse or harm, where 'it was for your good' is dangerous

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 43, chaupais 4-5 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 43.7-10). NOT 3.39: our id and label are off by four, and our text runs two chaupais.
attribution_note: Ram to Narada.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Continuing his answer to Narada, Ram compares the wise man (jnani) to a grown son and the humble servant to a small child: a mother still loves the grown son but no longer watches over him as before. The servant leans on Ram's strength, the jnani on his own, and both face desire and anger. So the wise keep devotion even after knowledge. The doha that follows names desire, anger, greed and pride as delusion's army.

key_terms.sense: even after gaining knowledge they don't give up devotion

core_teaching: Self-reliant wisdom leaves a person to fight desire and anger alone, while humble dependence on God brings his protection; so the wise keep devotion even after attaining knowledge.

commentaries.gist: Both the child and the servant are free of pride, and pride ruins both: it destroys the jnani's knowledge and the devotee's devotion.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 2), in Manas Piyush, citing Gita 3.37
commentaries.gist: Desire and anger are the enemy. Ram protected Narada from both, then let him fall to them when pride sprouted, to uproot the pride.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush, citing Gita 7.14 and 18.66
commentaries.gist: Maya is hard to cross except by taking refuge in the Lord; it lays many traps for the jnani, while the humble devotee is guarded.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that maturity and knowledge are good, but staying humble and connected protects us better than self-reliance alone.
misreadings: Not anti-intellectual: it asks the learned to keep humility, not to stop learning.
speaks_to: successful, self-reliant people feeling spiritually alone
not_for: someone who needs encouragement to become more independent

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Aranya Kand 46, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 46.1-2). NOT 3.42: our id and label are off by four.
attribution_note: Ram to Narada, describing the marks of saints (sadhus).
translation_note: Accurate. 'Sam' is even-minded (toward friend and foe), 'sital' cool, not heated by insults; 'niti' is right conduct.
context: After explaining why he stopped Narada's marriage, Ram is asked by Narada to describe the qualities of saints. Ram lists them over several lines: these come first, followed by japa, austerity and restraint, faith, forgiveness, friendliness, compassion, gladness, dispassion, discernment, humility, no hypocrisy or pride, love of his stories, and selfless service. He ends that not even Saraswati and the Vedas can tell them all. Narada departs, and the Aranya Kand closes.

key_terms.sense: shrink at hearing their own praise

core_teaching: Good people are embarrassed by praise of themselves and delighted by praise of others; they stay even and calm, keep to what is right, and are simple and kind with everyone.

commentaries.gist: Their praise is true, yet they shrink from it; the more they hear of others' virtues, the gladder they are. 'Even' toward friend and foe; 'cool' means harsh words from the wicked don't heat them.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Maps the list onto the four attitudes (friendliness, compassion, gladness, equanimity). Gladness at others' virtues is how one treats equals, which prevents envy and rivalry. Saints, unlike seekers, don't even practise indifference toward the wicked.
'Never leave right conduct' however things go; compares Lanka Kand, where a saint keeps to what is right despite a million obstacles.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a simple character checklist: deflect praise, celebrate others, keep your temper, stay honest and kind.
misreadings: Not a call for false modesty or refusing all recognition.
not_for: someone with very low self-esteem who already can't accept any praise

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand 3, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 3.1-2). NOT 4.4: our id and label are off by one (one too high).
attribution_note: Hanuman to Ram.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Parai jani bhore' is 'let (the servant) not fall from the master's memory'. Manas Piyush glosses: even if I have faults, don't forget your servant.
context: Sugriva, hiding on Rishyamuk hill, sends Hanuman disguised as a brahmin to find out who the two armed strangers are. Ram introduces himself. Hanuman recognises his Lord, falls at his feet, and says he failed to know him because he is deluded like any creature, then asks why Ram too forgot him. This line follows; he then says he knows no method of worship and relies on Ram like a child on its mother, and falls at Ram's feet in his own form.

key_terms.sense: let the master not forget the servant
is freed only by your tenderness

core_teaching: Hanuman admits many faults but asks not to be forgotten, since every being is bewildered by the Lord's power of illusion and can be freed only by his kindness.

commentaries.gist: Ordinary masters drop a servant on seeing faults; Ram is said never to count his people's faults, so he should not forget Hanuman either.
Hanuman's prayer contains the five things a seeker must know: the self (deluded by maya), the Lord, the obstacle (maya), the means (reliance on him), and the goal.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi (Vi. Tri.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He reasons: freedom comes only from your tenderness, and you seem to have forgotten me, and I have no practice of my own; this leaves him overwhelmed at Ram's feet.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that faults don't disqualify us from being loved, and that asking not to be forgotten is a valid prayer.
misreadings: Not a call to dwell on one's faults; the weight falls on the Lord's tenderness.
speaks_to: feeling forgotten by God or a mentor
not_for: someone who needs to hear about their strengths, not their faults

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand 3, chaupai 2 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 3.3-4). NOT 4.4: our id and label are off by one.
attribution_note: Hanuman to Ram.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Banai prabhu pose' means the master is bound to (has no choice but to) look after them.
context: Sugriva, hiding on Rishyamuk hill, sends Hanuman disguised as a brahmin to find out who the two armed strangers are. Ram introduces himself. Hanuman recognises his Lord, falls at his feet, and says he failed to know him because he is deluded like any creature, then asks why Ram too forgot him. Having asked not to be forgotten, he now confesses he knows no method of worship and states the principle of reliance.

key_terms.sense: the servant relying on the master, the child on the mother
the master has to look after them

core_teaching: Hanuman claims no spiritual technique, only reliance: as a servant trusts his master and a child its mother and so stays free of worry, the Lord is bound to care for one who depends on him.

commentaries.gist: There are two ways a deluded soul crosses maya: by the Lord's tenderness or by practice. Hanuman disclaims practice, so it must be grace. Escape from maya is achieved by grace, not effort.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ram Vallabhasharan, in Manas Piyush, citing Gita 9.22
commentaries.gist: 'Stays free of worry' means the dependent makes no plans for his own welfare; the Lord carries it, as Gita 9.22 promises.

commentaries.who: Prajnananand Saraswati (Pa. Pa. Pra.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: This is 'karpanya' surrender: the greatest devotee calling himself ignorant. Lessons: drop pride in one's own practices, and even stop worrying how or when one will be saved.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to relieve the pressure to 'do spirituality right': trust, like a child's trust in a parent, matters more than technique.
misreadings: Not a reason to stop acting or stay in harm's way (our misuse note is right).
Not an argument against practice; Hanuman is humble about his, not idle.
cautions: Someone who had unreliable parents may not find the child-mother image comforting.
speaks_to: anxiety about doing spiritual practice correctly
not_for: someone who was let down by a parent or carer

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand 3, chaupai 3 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 3.5-6). NOT 4.4: our id and label are off by one.
attribution_note: Narration (Shiva to Parvati in the Manas frame). 'Tulsidas -> the reader' is acceptable.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Nij tanu pragati' is 'revealing his own (monkey) form', dropping the brahmin disguise.
context: Sugriva, hiding on Rishyamuk hill, sends Hanuman disguised as a brahmin to find out who the two armed strangers are. Ram introduces himself. Hanuman recognises his Lord, falls at his feet, and says he failed to know him because he is deluded like any creature, then asks why Ram too forgot him. Here, having spoken, he falls at Ram's feet in his true form; Ram lifts and embraces him and then tells him not to feel small.

key_terms.sense: fell at his feet in distress
cooled him by bathing him with his tears

core_teaching: Once Hanuman drops his disguise and stands in his own form, Ram embraces him and soothes him with his own tears.

commentaries.who: Manas Mayank (Ma. Ma.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: He was distressed because Ram said nothing while he spoke. Ram would not accept anyone who came with a disguise; when love filled his heart the pretence fell away and Ram embraced him.

commentaries.who: Vijayanand Tripathi (Vi. Tri.), in Manas Piyush
commentaries.gist: Love cannot bear separation or concealment, so the true form appeared by itself once love filled him, as a disguised spy's real form appeared when he praised Ram.
Ram did not embrace him at the first fall but only after he dropped the brahmin guise: Ram doesn't like pretence. Ram's tears of love cooled the burning in Hanuman's heart.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to say that being accepted comes after we stop pretending: show up as you are.
speaks_to: being afraid to be seen as you are
not_for: someone who is unsafe being open about who they are

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand 3, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 3.7-8). NOT 4.4: our id and label are off by one.
attribution_note: Ram to Hanuman.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Una' is less, diminished.
context: Sugriva, hiding on Rishyamuk hill, sends Hanuman disguised as a brahmin to find out who the two armed strangers are. Ram introduces himself. Hanuman recognises his Lord, falls at his feet, and says he failed to know him because he is deluded like any creature, then asks why Ram too forgot him. Ram has just lifted him and held him; now he reassures him. The doha that follows defines the 'ananya' devotee: one who sees himself as servant and the whole world as the Lord's form.

key_terms.sense: don't feel small in your heart

core_teaching: Ram tells the ashamed Hanuman not to feel small: he is twice as dear as Lakshman. Ram is called impartial, but the servant with no other refuge is especially dear.

commentaries.gist: Ram's tears cooled Hanuman's anguish at thinking himself forgotten. Prajnananand reads the anguish as remorse for having approached Ram in disguise.
Ram uses the intimate singular 'tu' when most pleased with child-like servants, as he does with others he favours.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to lift shame: the one who feels most unworthy is told they are deeply valued. It also squares fairness with special love.
misreadings: Not a ranking that disparages Lakshman; it is said to lift Hanuman's shame.
speaks_to: feeling less loved than a sibling or colleague
not_for: someone hurt by favouritism
research_note: Manas Piyush notes on this exact line are shorter than for the lines before; both cited notes are on 3.3-3.4 as a unit.

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand 5, chaupai 4 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 5.7-8). NOT 4.6: our id and label are off by one.
attribution_note: Sugriva to Ram.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: After Ram and Sugriva swear friendship by fire, Sugriva says he once saw a woman being carried off crying 'Ram!', and shows the cloth she dropped. Ram clasps it to his chest and weeps. Sugriva tells him to set aside grief and promises to serve in every way until Sita is found. Ram then asks Sugriva why he lives in the forest, and hears about Bali.

key_terms.sense: I will serve in every way

core_teaching: Sugriva, himself exiled and separated from his wife, steadies the grieving Ram and pledges practical help. Comfort comes with a promise of action.

commentaries.gist: Valmiki's Sugriva says much the same at length: give up despair, remember your own steadiness; I too grieve for my wife but have not lost my composure; those ruled by grief find no happiness.
'Raghubir' reminds Ram he is a hero; grief undermines courage, so first let go of grief, then steadiness can come.
He says 'serve', not 'help', because he sees himself as servant. He forgets his own sorrow to comfort Ram, as Ram will forget his own to ask about Sugriva's.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for being a friend in grief: name the pain, then offer specific help rather than only words.
misreadings: 'Give up grief' here comes with a promise of help; it is not a demand to stop feeling.
cautions: Telling a grieving person to 'stop grieving' can hurt if not followed by real help.
speaks_to: mutual help between people who are both hurting
not_for: fresh bereavement, if 'give up grief' is read alone

verified_ref: Ramcharitmanas, Kishkindha Kand 7, chaupai 1 (Gita Press; Manas Piyush 7.1-2). NOT 4.8: our id and label are off by one.
attribution_note: Ram to Sugriva.
translation_note: First line misstated. 'Tinhahi bilokat pataka bhari' is literally 'just looking at them is a great sin'; Pt. Ramkumar explains it as contact with a great sinner. Our 'commit a grave wrong just by being seen' reverses the sense: it is the one who looks at them who incurs sin. Suggest: 'Even to look at those who are not pained by a friend's pain is a grave wrong.' The second line is fine.
context: Sugriva has told how his brother Bali drove him out and took his wife. Ram vows to kill Bali with one arrow. Then he sets out the duty of a friend: these lines, then steering a friend from wrong to right, revealing their virtues and hiding their faults, giving without hesitation, loving a hundredfold in hard times, and abandoning a friend who flatters to your face and harms behind your back.

key_terms.term: निज दुख गिरि सम रज करि जाना
key_terms.sense: seeing one's own mountain of sorrow as dust
a friend's speck of sorrow as Mount Meru

core_teaching: A true friend feels a friend's pain as their own, and treats their own huge troubles as small next to a friend's small ones. Ram then acts on this for Sugriva.

commentaries.who: Pt. Ramkumar (tippani 1), in Manas Piyush, citing Yajnavalkya Smriti
commentaries.gist: Those not pained by a friend's pain are great sinners, and association with great sinners makes one a sinner too, so one shouldn't even look at them.
Until you see your own sorrow as dust you won't feel a friend's as heavy or work to remove it. Ram is the example: exiled and bereft of Sita, he set that aside for Sugriva's trouble.
Those without this natural feeling should not force a friendship; a good friend turns you from wrong ways, shows your virtues and hides your faults, and loves a hundredfold in adversity.

practical_reading: Widely quoted on friendship: be moved by a friend's trouble, put your own in proportion, and show up when it matters.
misreadings: Not a demand to ignore your own suffering; it is about not letting it make you blind to a friend's.
Not a license to condemn people who couldn't help.
cautions: A carer already overwhelmed may hear 'your own pain is dust' as dismissal of their needs.
speaks_to: reflecting on who showed up for you
not_for: someone burned out from caring for others
someone whose friends abandoned them (could sting)
research_note: Our setting says 'as they swear friendship by the fire'; the fire oath was at Kishkindha 4, two dohas earlier. These lines come after Sugriva tells of Bali. Minor.
